title: Mozambique's LNG reset: from force majeure to major force | Wood Mackenzie
gist: Wood Mackenzie argues Mozambique's LNG sector is restarting, with up to US$45bn of investment and 38 mmtpa by 2032 if Rovuma LNG reaches FID by early 2027. Financing (about US$50bn external) and security remain key risks as 100+ mmtpa of global supply arrives by 2030.

insights.claim: If Rovuma LNG reaches FID by early 2027, Mozambique's four current projects could deliver 38 mmtpa of capacity by 2032, enough to overtake Nigeria as Africa's largest LNG exporter.
insights.speaker: Sayanima Kisku
insights.so_what: Shifts the African LNG supply hierarchy and the 2030s balance of Atlantic vs Indian Ocean supply.

insights.claim: Coral Sul, the world's fifth FLNG project, has run at its 3.4 mmtpa capacity since reaching plateau in 2023, giving Area 4 partners confidence to sanction the enhanced replica Coral Norte targeting first LNG in 2028.
insights.speaker: Sayanima Kisku
insights.so_what: Proven FLNG execution de-risks replica projects and supports the FLNG-first development model.
insights.locator: From force majeure to four projects

insights.claim: TotalEnergies' 13.1 mmtpa Mozambique LNG, sanctioned in 2019, suffered four and a half years of force majeure from 2021; construction restarted in January 2026, the project is about 45% complete and start-up is targeted for 2029.
insights.speaker: Sayanima Kisku
insights.so_what: Restart removes a major overhang on TotalEnergies' growth pipeline, though 2029 timing remains exposed to security.
insights.locator: From force majeure to four projects

insights.claim: ExxonMobil redesigned Rovuma LNG during the delay, replacing two large trains with 12 mini-trains to lift capacity to 18.6 mmtpa; FID is targeted for late 2026 at about US$27 billion, which would make it Africa's largest-ever energy development.
insights.speaker: Sayanima Kisku
insights.so_what: Rovuma FID is the key near-term catalyst for Exxon's LNG growth and the sector's financing market.
insights.locator: From force majeure to four projects

insights.claim: Mozambique's exploration boom in the early 2010s found 125 tcf across Areas 1 and 4, enough for a separate LNG project in each block.
insights.speaker: Sayanima Kisku
insights.so_what: Resource base is large enough to support multiple phases beyond current projects.
insights.locator: From force majeure to four projects

insights.claim: Around US$45 billion could be invested in 2026-2033 to complete Coral Norte and the two onshore projects.
insights.speaker: Sayanima Kisku
insights.so_what: Large contract and services pipeline for EPC, FLNG and subsea suppliers.

insights.claim: About 75 tcf remains uncommercialised across Areas 1 and 4, enough for Mozambique LNG Phase 2, a third Area 4 FLNG vessel and possibly a joint development of straddling resources, adding 30-35 mmtpa.
insights.speaker: Sayanima Kisku
insights.so_what: Implies a multi-decade growth runway beyond the first four projects.

insights.claim: Follow-on projects could push Mozambique's output above 70 mmtpa by 2040, making it the world's fourth-largest LNG producer ahead of Canada, with cumulative investment above US$90 billion over 2026-2040.
insights.speaker: Sayanima Kisku
insights.so_what: Mozambique would become a structural competitor to Canadian and other new LNG supply.

insights.claim: Mozambique's location outside the Persian Gulf and proximity to South Asia make it more attractive as recent geopolitical disruption reshapes buyers' risk calculations.
insights.speaker: Sayanima Kisku
insights.so_what: Supply-security premium favors non-Gulf LNG, supporting offtake demand from Asian buyers.
insights.locator: Why the majors and Asian buyers

insights.claim: Asian national oil companies including CNPC, PTTEP and three Indian NOCs, plus ADNOC's XRG, are non-operating partners in Areas 1 and 4.
insights.speaker: Sayanima Kisku
insights.so_what: Asian and Gulf state capital is deeply embedded, which aids financing and offtake alignment.
insights.locator: Why the majors and Asian buyers

insights.claim: Mozambique could account for 16% of Eni's upstream value by 2030, and could become TotalEnergies' highest-value African country and CNPC's most valuable position worldwide if all projects proceed.
insights.speaker: Sayanima Kisku
insights.so_what: Equity exposure to Mozambique execution is material for Eni, TotalEnergies and CNPC.
insights.locator: Why the majors and Asian buyers

insights.claim: Cabo Delgado conditions have improved but remain uncertain, and government approvals for Mozambique LNG's revised budget and Rovuma LNG's amended development plan are still outstanding.
insights.speaker: Sayanima Kisku
insights.so_what: Security and approvals are gating risks for the FID and schedule.

insights.claim: Mozambique's newly amended Petroleum Law creates uncertainty over domestic gas obligations and pricing.
insights.speaker: Sayanima Kisku
insights.so_what: Fiscal and domestic-market terms could erode project returns.

insights.claim: Total capex could exceed US$75 billion if Rovuma LNG and the three follow-on projects proceed, with about US$50 billion needed from external lenders, which Wood Mackenzie calls potentially the biggest test.
insights.speaker: Sayanima Kisku
insights.so_what: Large lender demand makes bank and ECA appetite the swing factor for timing.

insights.claim: Over 100 mmtpa of new global LNG capacity is set to reach the market by 2030, so every year of delay narrows Mozambique's window before that supply wave arrives.
insights.speaker: Sayanima Kisku
insights.so_what: Delay risks arriving into a looser market, pressuring pricing and returns.
